title: Why You Should Limit Discussion In Your Classroom ssroom/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that classroom discussion, while not worthless, is vastly overused relative to actual student work, largely because leading a discussion feels and looks like effective teaching while letting many students remain passive and hide. He distinguishes productive uses of discussion, such as coordinating academic project work, structured review where all students are called on, or formal Socratic seminars, from the common, low-value prompts that produce what he calls 'virtually zero learning.' The article extends this critique to debate, arguing it's valuable only when backed by researched, written position papers, not casual talk. He proposes replacing lazy discussion prompts with real, individual or group work that requires active analysis, writing, or problem-solving, framing this shift as more engaging and effective for students. The piece closes with a rapid list of the qualities that should replace passive discussion time: active learning, involvement, challenge, and doing.
points: Classroom discussion is overused relative to actual work because leading a discussion feels like teaching, and it's easy for many students to passively hide within it.
Legitimate uses of discussion include coordinating academic project work, structured review where all students are called on, and formal Socratic seminars.
Common discussion prompts, such as casual partner talk about a story or vote, are described as producing virtually zero real learning.
Debate is only valuable when backed by researched, written position papers; otherwise it becomes a largely wasted exercise.
Replacing passive discussion with real individual or group work, such as analyzing, solving, or creating, produces more engagement and better learning outcomes.
quotes: It’s not that all discussion should be thrown out. It’s just that the proportion of it compared to actual work is too high.
The reason for this is that it feels like teaching. You’re up there doing your thing, pacing, talking loudly, in control. It’s also easy and appears from the outside as if you’re a good teacher.

These prompts and millions like them accomplish almost nothing. Virtually zero learning. Listen to your students as they discuss these soft queries. It’s cringe-inducing how little they understand and how far off track they go.

Debate only works if students research their ideas and back them up with arguments and evidence. They must be prepared by writing out position papers and having their ideas challenged or it’s a colossal waste of time.
Active learning. Involvement. Challenge. Responsibility. Discomfort. Preparation. Objective. Doing. Every directed lesson should provide the assignment and tools needed to succeed.
